courses.title: Network Fundamentals
courses.description: Build a rock-solid mental model of networking — network types and topologies, the OSI and TCP/IP models, encapsulation, protocols and ports, and the physical media that carry the data.

content.intro: A network is two or more devices connected to share data and resources. Everything else in networking builds on a few basic shapes and roles.

ul.t: a local area network — one site (office, home).
a wide area network spanning sites/cities (the internet is the biggest WAN).

p: Physical/logical layouts — star (switch-centred, the modern default), mesh (many redundant links), bus and ring (legacy). Star dominates because a single failed cable affects only one device.

content.practice: Sketch your home or office as a network: identify the LAN, what connects it to the WAN, and which devices are clients vs servers.

quiz.p: The internet is best described as…
quiz.ex: The internet is a global wide area network (WAN).

quiz.p: In a star topology, devices connect to…
quiz.ex: Star topologies centre on a switch; the modern default.

quiz.p: A device that both requests and provides resources is…
quiz.ex: Peer-to-peer devices act as both client and server.

content.intro: The OSI model breaks networking into seven layers. It's the shared language technicians use to describe where a problem lives.

sections.caption: The OSI model: seven layers and the data unit (PDU) at each.

note.text: Troubleshoot layer by layer: is it physical (cable/link), addressing (IP), or application? Naming the layer focuses the fix.

content.practice: For a 'can't reach the website' problem, list one thing you'd check at layers 1, 3, and 7.

quiz.p: Routing and IP addressing happen at which OSI layer?
quiz.ex: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical addressing and routing.

quiz.p: MAC addresses and switching operate at layer…
quiz.ex: Layer 2 (Data Link) uses MAC addresses; switches work here.

quiz.p: The data unit at the Transport layer is a…
quiz.ex: Layer 4 works with segments (TCP) / datagrams (UDP).

content.intro: The practical model the internet actually runs on is TCP/IP. Encapsulation is how your data gets wrapped for delivery and unwrapped on arrival.

p: Four layers — Application, Transport, Internet, and Network Access — map onto the OSI layers but reflect how real protocols are built.

sections.caption: Each layer adds its own header (and the frame adds a trailer) as data moves down the stack.

p: Going down the stack, each layer adds a header; the receiver reverses the process (de-encapsulation) going back up. Routers read the IP header; switches read the frame header.

content.practice: Explain in one sentence what a router reads to forward traffic versus what a switch reads.

quiz.p: Encapsulation means each layer…
o: Adds its own header as data moves down
quiz.ex: Each layer prepends its header on the way down the stack.

quiz.p: A router makes forwarding decisions using the…
quiz.ex: Routers read the layer-3 IP header to route packets.

quiz.p: The TCP/IP model has how many layers?
quiz.ex: The TCP/IP model is commonly described as four layers.

content.intro: Protocols are the rules; ports are the numbered doors that let one host run many services at once.

ul.t: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered (web, email, file transfer).
connectionless, fast, best-effort (DNS queries, VoIP, streaming).

note.text: 0-1023 are well-known, 1024-49151 registered, 49152-65535 dynamic/ephemeral (used by clients).

content.practice: List the protocol and transport (TCP/UDP) for: loading a secure website, a DNS lookup, and a remote desktop session.

quiz.p: Which transport protocol is reliable and connection-oriented?
quiz.ex: TCP provides reliable, ordered, connection-oriented delivery.

quiz.p: HTTPS uses which port by default?
quiz.ex: HTTPS uses TCP port 443.

quiz.p: DNS queries typically use which transport for speed?
quiz.ex: DNS uses UDP/53 for most queries, with TCP for large responses/zone transfers.

content.intro: The physical layer still matters — the wrong cable or a bad run causes 'mystery' problems no software fix can solve.

ul.t: 1 Gbps up to 10 Gbps over limited distances (~100 m max run).
most modern gear auto-detects (Auto-MDIX), but know the difference.

note.text: Copper for the desk, fiber for distance and backbones or where electrical interference is a problem.

content.practice: For a 300-metre link between two buildings, decide copper vs fiber and justify it in one line.

quiz.p: The practical maximum run for twisted-pair copper is about…
quiz.ex: Twisted-pair Ethernet runs are limited to roughly 100 m.

quiz.p: For a long-distance campus backbone you'd choose…
quiz.ex: Single-mode fiber covers long distances.

quiz.p: Auto-MDIX means…
quiz.ex: Auto-MDIX removes the need to pick crossover vs straight-through.

courses.title: IPv4 Addressing & Subnetting
courses.description: Master IPv4 the way the job demands — addressing and private ranges, subnet masks and CIDR, subnetting by hand, VLSM, and designing an addressing scheme that scales.

content.intro: An IPv4 address is 32 bits written as four decimal octets. Every address splits into a network part and a host part.

ul: 32 bits = four 8-bit octets (0-255), e.g. 192.168.1.10
A subnet mask marks which bits are network vs host
Network address = all host bits 0; broadcast = all host bits 1

note.text: Private addresses aren't routable on the internet; NAT translates them to a public address at the edge.

content.practice: Identify whether these are public or private: 10.4.5.6, 8.8.8.8, 172.20.1.1, 192.168.0.50.

quiz.p: An IPv4 address is how many bits?
quiz.ex: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits (four octets).

quiz.p: Which is a private (RFC 1918) range?
quiz.ex: 172.16.0.0/12 is private; 10/8 and 192.168/16 are the others.

quiz.p: The network address of a subnet has all host bits set to…
quiz.ex: All host bits 0 = the network address; all 1 = broadcast.

content.intro: The subnet mask (and its CIDR shorthand) is what actually divides an address into network and host. Read it fluently and subnetting becomes easy.

sections.caption: A /27 prefix: 27 network bits and 5 host bits → mask 255.255.255.224.

note.text: Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2 (subtracting network and broadcast). A /27 has 2^5−2 = 30 hosts.

content.practice: Without a calculator, give the mask and usable host count for /26 and /28.

quiz.p: A /24 network provides how many usable hosts?
quiz.ex: 256 addresses minus network and broadcast = 254 usable.

quiz.p: The mask 255.255.255.224 corresponds to which prefix?
Usable hosts per subnet is calculated as…
quiz.ex: Subtract network and broadcast addresses.

content.intro: Subnetting borrows host bits to create multiple smaller networks — the core skill for segmenting and sizing networks.

p: Every bit you borrow doubles the number of subnets and halves the hosts per subnet. Design around the larger of 'subnets needed' or 'hosts per subnet needed'.

ul: Block size = 256 − mask octet (e.g. /27 → 256−224 = 32)
Subnets start at multiples of the block: 0, 32, 64, 96 …
The network an address belongs to is the block it falls into

p: 192.168.10.37 /27: block size 32 → networks at .0, .32, .64… .37 falls in the .32 block, so network = 192.168.10.32, broadcast = .63, usable .33–.62.

note.text: This block-size method lets you subnet in your head — no binary conversion required for most questions.

content.practice: For 10.20.30.100/26, work out the network address, broadcast, and usable host range by hand, then check it.

quiz.p: Borrowing one more host bit for subnets…
quiz.ex: Each borrowed bit doubles subnets and halves hosts per subnet.

quiz.p: For a /27, the block size in the last octet is…
192.168.10.37/27 belongs to which network?
quiz.ex: Block size 32; .37 falls in the .32 subnet.

content.intro: Speed comes from reps. This lesson drills the repeatable method you can apply to any address.

ul: 1. From the prefix, find host bits and the mask octet
2. Block size = 256 − mask octet
3. List subnet boundaries (multiples of block size)
4. Your address's network = the boundary it falls in; broadcast = next boundary − 1
5. Usable range = network+1 to broadcast−1

note.text: Network and broadcast are never usable host addresses — if you assign one to a host, connectivity breaks.

content.practice: Solve three of your own: pick random addresses with /26, /28, and /30 and compute network, broadcast, and host range.

quiz.p: 172.16.5.200/28 has which broadcast address?
quiz.ex: Block size 16; .200 is in .192, broadcast = .207.

quiz.p: A /30 subnet provides how many usable hosts?
quiz.ex: /30 = 4 addresses − 2 = 2 usable (ideal for point-to-point links).

quiz.p: The last usable host in 10.0.5.130/25 is…
quiz.ex: Network .128, broadcast .255, so last usable is .254.

content.intro: Real networks have subnets of different sizes. VLSM lets you fit the mask to each subnet's need instead of wasting addresses.

p: A fixed mask wastes space — a point-to-point link doesn't need 254 hosts. VLSM assigns the right-sized subnet to each requirement.

ul: Sort requirements largest-to-smallest by host count
Assign each the smallest subnet that fits (round up to a power of two)
Carve them from the address space in order, without overlap

note.text: From 192.168.1.0/24: a 100-host LAN takes a /25, a 50-host LAN a /26 from the remainder, and point-to-point links take /30s — no overlap, minimal waste.

content.practice: Given 192.168.1.0/24 and needs of 100, 50, 25, and two 2-host links, allocate subnets with VLSM (no overlaps).

quiz.p: VLSM is used to…
o: Right-size each subnet to its host need
quiz.ex: VLSM fits the mask to each subnet, reducing waste.

quiz.p: When applying VLSM you allocate…
quiz.ex: Allocate largest-to-smallest to avoid fragmentation.

quiz.p: A 2-host point-to-point link is best served by a…
quiz.ex: /30 gives exactly two usable hosts.

content.intro: A good addressing plan is documented, leaves room to grow, and encodes meaning so humans can read the network.

ul: Reserve blocks per site/VLAN/purpose (e.g. servers, users, voice)
Leave headroom for growth — don't allocate to the last address
Keep it summarisable so routing stays simple

p: Encode meaning: e.g. 10.<site>.<vlan>.<host>. Consistency turns an IP into information.

note.text: An undocumented scheme becomes unmanageable fast. Maintain IPAM/records of every subnet's purpose and range.

content.practice: Draft an addressing scheme for a two-site company with users, servers, and voice VLANs, leaving room to double in size.

quiz.p: A good addressing scheme should…
o: Leave headroom for growth and be documented
quiz.ex: Plan for growth and document it.

quiz.p: Summarisable (contiguous) allocation helps…
o: Keep routing tables small and simple
quiz.ex: Summarisation reduces routing complexity.

quiz.p: Encoding site/VLAN into the address makes it…
quiz.ex: Structured addressing conveys meaning to operators.

courses.title: IPv6 Essentials
courses.description: Understand the address space that's replacing IPv4 — 128-bit addressing and notation, address types and autoconfiguration, and how IPv6 coexists with IPv4.

content.intro: IPv4 ran out of addresses. IPv6 uses 128 bits — an effectively unlimited space — written in hexadecimal.

ul: 128 bits shown as eight groups of four hex digits, separated by colons

ul.b: Replace one run of all-zero groups with ::

note.text: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329 is the shortened form of the address above — far more manageable.

quiz.p: An IPv6 address is how many bits?
quiz.ex: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.

quiz.p: The :: in an IPv6 address may appear…
quiz.ex: A double colon compresses one run of zero groups, used once.

quiz.p: IPv6 addresses are written in…
quiz.ex: IPv6 uses hexadecimal groups separated by colons.

content.intro: IPv6 has several address scopes and can configure itself without DHCP.

ul.t: auto-assigned, valid on the local link only.

p: SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets a host build its own address from a router-advertised prefix. DHCPv6 is available when you need central control.

note.text: IPv6 replaces broadcast with multicast — more efficient. Every interface also gets a link-local fe80 address automatically.

content.practice: On any device, find its IPv6 link-local (fe80) address and note which interface it's on.

quiz.p: A link-local IPv6 address starts with…
quiz.ex: Link-local addresses use fe80::/10.

quiz.p: SLAAC allows a host to…
o: Auto-configure its address from a router prefix
quiz.ex: SLAAC builds an address from the advertised prefix, no DHCP needed.

quiz.p: IPv6 replaces broadcast with…
quiz.ex: IPv6 uses multicast instead of broadcast.

content.intro: The internet won't switch overnight, so IPv4 and IPv6 run side by side using a few coexistence techniques.

ul.t: run IPv4 and IPv6 together (the preferred, simplest path).
carry IPv6 across IPv4-only networks (6in4, etc.).
let IPv6-only hosts reach IPv4 services.

note.text: Dual-stack is the dominant strategy: hosts prefer IPv6 when both are available and fall back to IPv4.

content.practice: State which coexistence method you'd use to let a new IPv6-only network reach legacy IPv4-only servers.

quiz.p: The preferred, simplest coexistence method is…
quiz.ex: Running both stacks (dual-stack) is the common approach.

quiz.p: NAT64 is used to…
o: Let IPv6-only hosts reach IPv4 services
quiz.ex: NAT64 translates between IPv6-only clients and IPv4 servers.

quiz.p: Tunneling helps when…
o: IPv6 must cross an IPv4-only network
quiz.ex: Tunnels carry IPv6 over IPv4-only paths.

courses.title: Switching & VLANs
courses.description: How local networks really move frames — Ethernet and MAC addressing, VLAN segmentation, 802.1Q trunking, spanning tree, and switch security.

content.intro: Switches forward Ethernet frames using MAC addresses. Understanding this layer-2 behaviour explains most LAN issues.

p: A 48-bit hardware address burned into each NIC (e.g. 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E). Switches learn which MAC lives on which port and build a MAC address table.

ul: Known destination MAC → forward out that one port
Unknown/broadcast → flood out all ports (except the source)
Learns source MACs to fill its table

note.text: ARP maps a known IP to its MAC on the local network — the glue between layer 3 addressing and layer 2 delivery.

content.practice: On a device, view the ARP table (arp -a) and identify the MAC of your default gateway.

quiz.p: A switch forwards frames based on…
quiz.ex: Switches use layer-2 MAC addresses.

quiz.p: When a switch doesn't know the destination MAC it…
o: Floods it out all other ports
quiz.ex: Unknown-unicast frames are flooded until the MAC is learned.

quiz.p: ARP resolves…
o: IP to MAC on the local network
quiz.ex: ARP finds the MAC for a known local IP.

content.intro: VLANs split one physical switch into multiple logical networks — the foundation of segmentation.

p: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain. Devices in different VLANs can't talk without a router, even on the same switch — great for isolating departments, voice, and guests.
An access port belongs to a single VLAN and connects an end device (PC, printer, phone).

sections.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="ui-sans-serif,system-ui" font-size="12"><rect x="60" y="90" width="120" height="40" rx="6" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#475569"/><text x="120" y="115" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">Switch A</text><rect x="380" y="90" width="120" height="40" rx="6" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#475569"/><text x="440" y="115" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">Switch B</text><line x1="180" y1="110" x2="380" y2="110" stroke="#818cf8" stroke-width="3"/><text x="280" y="102" fill="#a5b4fc" text-anchor="middle">802.1Q trunk</text><text x="280" y="126" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle">carries VLAN 10 + 20</text><circle cx="40" cy="70" r="10" fill="#2563eb"/><line x1="50" y1="74" x2="70" y2="100" stroke="#2563eb"/><circle cx="520" cy="70" r="10" fill="#2563eb"/><line x1="510" y1="74" x2="490" y2="100" stroke="#2563eb"/><text x="40" y="50" fill="#93c5fd" text-anchor="middle">VLAN 10</text><text x="520" y="50" fill="#93c5fd" text-anchor="middle">VLAN 10</text><circle cx="40" cy="160" r="10" fill="#16a34a"/><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="70" y2="122" stroke="#16a34a"/><circle cx="520" cy="160" r="10" fill="#16a34a"/><line x1="510" y1="156" x2="490" y2="122" stroke="#16a34a"/><text x="40" y="188" fill="#86efac" text-anchor="middle">VLAN 20</text><text x="520" y="188" fill="#86efac" text-anchor="middle">VLAN 20</text></svg>
sections.caption: Access ports place devices into VLAN 10 or 20; a trunk carries both VLANs between switches.

note.text: VLANs improve security and performance by containing broadcasts and separating traffic — without extra hardware.

content.practice: Design a VLAN plan for an office with staff, guests, and IP phones, and state why each is separated.

quiz.p: Each VLAN is a separate…
quiz.ex: A VLAN is its own broadcast domain.

quiz.p: Devices in different VLANs communicate via…
quiz.ex: Inter-VLAN traffic must be routed.

quiz.p: An access port carries…
o: A single VLAN to an end device
quiz.ex: Access ports belong to one VLAN for an end device.

content.intro: A trunk carries many VLANs over one link between switches (or to a router), using tags to keep them separate.

p: The trunk inserts a VLAN tag into each frame so the far end knows which VLAN it belongs to. This lets a single cable carry dozens of VLANs.
One VLAN on a trunk is 'native' and sent untagged. Match it on both ends and avoid using VLAN 1 for it as a hardening step.

note.text: Switch-to-switch links, switch-to-router (router-on-a-stick), and switch-to-hypervisor uplinks are all trunks.

content.practice: Explain what tag a frame for VLAN 20 carries across a trunk, and what happens to native-VLAN frames.

quiz.p: 802.1Q trunks keep VLANs separate by…
o: Inserting a VLAN tag in each frame
quiz.ex: The 802.1Q tag identifies each frame's VLAN.

quiz.p: The native VLAN on a trunk is…
quiz.ex: Native-VLAN traffic is sent untagged; match both ends.

quiz.p: A trunk link is typically used for…
quiz.ex: Trunks interconnect infrastructure carrying multiple VLANs.

content.intro: Redundant switch links can create loops that melt a network. Spanning Tree prevents them automatically.

p: Layer-2 loops have no TTL, so broadcasts circulate forever — a 'broadcast storm' that saturates the LAN.
STP elects a root bridge and blocks redundant paths, leaving one loop-free active path. If a link fails, a blocked path is unblocked to restore connectivity.

note.text: Rapid STP (RSTP) converges in seconds. Use PortFast on access ports and BPDU Guard to protect the topology.

content.practice: Describe what happens without STP when you connect two switches with two cables, and how STP prevents it.

quiz.p: Layer-2 loops are dangerous because frames…
o: Have no TTL and can circulate forever
quiz.ex: No TTL at layer 2 means loops cause broadcast storms.

quiz.p: Spanning Tree prevents loops by…
o: Blocking redundant paths, leaving one active
quiz.ex: STP blocks redundant links to keep a loop-free topology.

quiz.p: Which improves convergence and protects access ports?
quiz.ex: RSTP plus PortFast/BPDU Guard is best practice.

content.intro: The access layer is where users (and attackers) plug in. A few switch features close common gaps.

p: Limit which/how many MAC addresses a port accepts, and shut or restrict the port on violation — stopping rogue hubs and MAC flooding.

ul.t: and put them in an unused VLAN.

note.text: Never leave default credentials or unencrypted management (Telnet) — use SSH and change defaults.

content.practice: List three switch-hardening steps you'd apply to an office access switch and the threat each addresses.

quiz.p: Port security can…
o: Limit MAC addresses per port and act on violations
quiz.ex: It restricts MACs per port to stop rogue devices/flooding.

quiz.p: Which stops a rogue DHCP server on the access layer?
quiz.ex: DHCP snooping permits DHCP only from trusted ports.

quiz.p: Unused switch ports should be…
o: Disabled / placed in an unused VLAN
quiz.ex: Disabling unused ports reduces attack surface.

courses.title: Routing
courses.description: Move traffic between networks — routing tables and decisions, static and dynamic routing, inter-VLAN routing, and NAT/PAT.

content.intro: Routers connect different networks and choose the best path for each packet using a routing table.

ul: Each entry maps a destination network to a next hop / exit interface
The router picks the most specific match (longest prefix match)
A default route (0.0.0.0/0) catches everything else

p: Each router forwards to the next hop toward the destination network, hop by hop, until delivery — it only cares about the destination network, not the whole path.

note.text: A host sends off-subnet traffic to its default gateway (a router), which takes over the forwarding decision.

content.practice: On a device, view the routing table (route print / ip route) and identify the default route and gateway.

quiz.p: A router selects a route using…
quiz.ex: Longest-prefix match picks the most specific route.

quiz.p: The default route is written as…
quiz.ex: 0.0.0.0/0 matches any destination not matched more specifically.

quiz.p: A host sends traffic for another subnet to its…
quiz.ex: Off-subnet traffic goes to the default gateway (router).

content.intro: Static routes are manually configured paths — simple, predictable, and ideal for small or stub networks.

ul: Small networks with few paths
Stub networks (one way in/out)
A default route to the internet edge

p: Static routes don't adapt automatically — if a link fails or the topology changes, you must update them by hand. They add no protocol overhead, though.

content.practice: Write the static route a branch router needs to reach 10.5.5.0/24 through next hop 10.0.0.2.

quiz.p: Static routing is best for…
quiz.ex: Static routes suit small/stub topologies.

quiz.p: A drawback of static routing is that it…
quiz.ex: Static routes must be updated manually when the topology changes.

quiz.p: A route to 0.0.0.0/0 is a…
quiz.ex: 0.0.0.0/0 is the default route.

content.intro: Dynamic routing protocols let routers learn and adapt paths automatically — essential as networks grow.

ul.t: share their whole table with neighbours; simple, slower to converge.
build a full map and compute best paths; faster, more scalable.
how a protocol rates a path (hop count, bandwidth, cost).
how fast all routers agree after a change.

note.text: OSPF is the common interior link-state protocol; BGP runs between organisations and powers internet routing.

content.practice: Explain in one line why a link-state protocol like OSPF converges faster than a basic distance-vector protocol.

quiz.p: OSPF is which type of routing protocol?
quiz.ex: OSPF is a link-state interior gateway protocol.

quiz.p: Convergence refers to…
o: How fast routers agree after a topology change
quiz.ex: Convergence is the time to reach a consistent routing view.

quiz.p: The protocol that routes between organisations on the internet is…
quiz.ex: BGP is the internet's inter-domain routing protocol.

content.intro: VLANs isolate traffic, so something must route between them. Two designs do the job.

p: A single trunk to a router carries all VLANs; the router has a sub-interface per VLAN and routes between them. Simple, but the one link can bottleneck.
A multilayer switch routes between VLANs internally using Switched Virtual Interfaces (SVIs) — faster and the usual enterprise choice.

note.text: Each VLAN gets a gateway IP (the router sub-interface or the SVI) that its hosts use as their default gateway.

content.practice: Decide router-on-a-stick vs a layer-3 switch for a 6-VLAN office and justify the choice.

quiz.p: Router-on-a-stick routes VLANs using…
quiz.ex: A trunk with per-VLAN sub-interfaces routes between VLANs.

quiz.p: A layer-3 switch routes between VLANs with…
quiz.ex: SVIs give the switch a routed interface per VLAN.

quiz.p: Each VLAN's hosts use which as their default gateway?
o: The router sub-interface or SVI for that VLAN
quiz.ex: The per-VLAN routed interface is the gateway.

content.intro: NAT lets many private hosts share public addresses — the reason IPv4 didn't run out sooner.

p: Network Address Translation rewrites private source addresses to a public one at the network edge, and reverses it for return traffic.

sections.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 580 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="ui-sans-serif,system-ui" font-size="12"><rect x="20" y="40" width="130" height="30" rx="5" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#475569"/><text x="85" y="60" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">PC 192.168.1.10</text><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="30" rx="5" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#475569"/><text x="85" y="140" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">PC 192.168.1.11</text><line x1="150" y1="55" x2="250" y2="90" stroke="#64748b"/><line x1="150" y1="135" x2="250" y2="100" stroke="#64748b"/><rect x="250" y="75" width="110" height="44" rx="8" fill="#3730a3" stroke="#818cf8"/><text x="305" y="93" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">Router</text><text x="305" y="110" fill="#c7d2fe" text-anchor="middle">NAT / PAT</text><line x1="360" y1="97" x2="450" y2="97" stroke="#64748b"/><rect x="450" y="78" width="110" height="40" rx="8" fill="#0f172a" stroke="#475569"/><text x="505" y="95" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">Internet</text><text x="505" y="111" fill="#94a3b8" text-anchor="middle">203.0.113.5</text><text x="290" y="150" fill="#64748b">many private IPs → one public IP (different ports)</text></svg>
sections.caption: PAT maps many private IPs to one public IP, using port numbers to tell sessions apart.

note.text: Almost every home/office uses PAT: many internal devices behind a single public IP. It also hides internal addressing from the internet.

content.practice: Describe how the router tells apart return traffic for two PCs that both browsed the web through one public IP.

quiz.p: NAT primarily translates…
quiz.ex: NAT rewrites private↔public addresses at the edge.

quiz.p: PAT distinguishes many hosts behind one public IP using…
quiz.ex: PAT uses unique port numbers per session.

quiz.p: A side benefit of NAT is that it…
o: Hides internal addressing from the internet
quiz.ex: Internal addresses aren't exposed publicly.

courses.title: Wireless Networking
courses.description: Deliver reliable Wi-Fi — the 802.11 standards and bands, wireless security, and designing and troubleshooting coverage.

content.intro: Wi-Fi performance depends on the standard and the radio band. Knowing them explains speed and coverage trade-offs.

ul.t: efficiency in dense areas, adds 6 GHz.
longer range, more interference, fewer non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11).

note.text: On 2.4 GHz stick to channels 1, 6, and 11 to avoid overlap — the most common cause of home Wi-Fi interference.

content.practice: Check which band and channel your Wi-Fi uses and whether neighbours are overlapping your 2.4 GHz channel.

quiz.p: Which band offers longer range but more interference?
quiz.ex: 2.4 GHz reaches further but is more congested.

quiz.p: The non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels are…
quiz.ex: Channels 1, 6, 11 don't overlap on 2.4 GHz.

quiz.p: Wi-Fi 6E adds which band?
quiz.ex: Wi-Fi 6E extends into the 6 GHz band.

content.intro: Wireless is a shared medium anyone nearby can hear, so encryption and authentication are essential.

ul.t: current standard, stronger protection against offline attacks.
a shared passphrase — simple, fine for home/small sites.
per-user credentials via RADIUS — the business standard.

note.text: Isolate guest Wi-Fi from the internal network (its own VLAN) and enable client isolation.

content.practice: Recommend the encryption and auth mode for (a) a home network and (b) a company office, and justify each.

quiz.p: The current strongest common Wi-Fi encryption is…
quiz.ex: WPA3 is the current standard; WEP/WPA are insecure.

quiz.p: Enterprise Wi-Fi authentication (802.1X) uses…
quiz.ex: 802.1X authenticates each user, typically via RADIUS.

quiz.p: Guest Wi-Fi should be…
o: Isolated on its own VLAN with client isolation
quiz.ex: Isolate guests from internal resources.

content.intro: Good Wi-Fi is engineered, not guessed. Coverage, interference, and capacity all need planning.

ul: Survey for coverage and place APs to overlap slightly
Plan channels to avoid co-channel interference
Size for device density, not just area

ul.t: clients sticking to a far AP.

note.text: In business networks, a wireless controller (or cloud) manages many APs centrally for consistent config, channel planning, and roaming.

content.practice: For a two-floor office with weak coverage in corners, list three things you'd check or change.

quiz.p: A common 2.4 GHz interference source is…
quiz.ex: 2.4 GHz shares spectrum with microwaves and Bluetooth.

quiz.p: Wireless capacity should be sized for…
quiz.ex: Dense client counts, not just coverage, drive AP planning.

quiz.p: A wireless controller is used to…
quiz.ex: Controllers manage AP config, channels, and roaming centrally.

courses.title: Network Security & Services
courses.description: Protect and serve the network — firewalls and ACLs, VPNs and IPsec, segmentation and zero-trust, and the DNS/DHCP services every network relies on.

content.intro: Firewalls and access control lists decide what traffic is allowed where — the network's front door.

p: A stateful firewall tracks connections and allows return traffic automatically, blocking anything not part of an allowed session. It's the standard perimeter and inter-zone control.

ul: Permit/deny rules matched by source, destination, port, protocol
Order matters — first match wins
End with an implicit deny

note.text: Default-deny, then explicitly allow what's needed. Group interfaces into zones (inside, outside, DMZ) and control traffic between them.

content.practice: Write, in plain rules, an ACL that allows web traffic to a server but blocks everything else to it.

quiz.p: A stateful firewall…
o: Tracks connections and allows return traffic
quiz.ex: Stateful firewalls track sessions and permit their return traffic.

quiz.p: In an ACL, rule order matters because…
quiz.ex: ACLs evaluate top-down; the first match applies.

quiz.p: A secure default firewall policy is…
quiz.ex: Default-deny with explicit allows is best practice.

content.intro: VPNs create encrypted tunnels across untrusted networks so remote users and sites connect securely.

note.text: SSL/TLS VPNs (over 443) are firewall-friendly for remote users; IPsec is common for site-to-site.

content.practice: Decide site-to-site vs remote-access VPN for (a) linking two offices and (b) home workers, and why.

quiz.p: A site-to-site VPN connects…
quiz.ex: Site-to-site links entire networks.

quiz.p: IPsec tunnel mode encrypts…
quiz.ex: Tunnel mode encapsulates and encrypts the whole packet.

quiz.p: IPsec provides confidentiality, integrity, and…
quiz.ex: IPsec authenticates peers alongside encrypting/integrity-checking traffic.

content.intro: Flat networks let one compromise reach everything. Segmentation and zero-trust limit the blast radius.

p: Divide the network into zones (users, servers, IoT, guest) with controlled traffic between them, so a breach in one can't freely reach others. VLANs + firewall/ACLs implement it.
A demilitarised zone hosts internet-facing services in a separate segment, isolated from the internal network.

note.text: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust by location — verify identity and authorise every access, and microsegment east-west traffic.

content.practice: Propose three segments for a small business and the traffic you'd allow between them.

quiz.p: Network segmentation primarily…
o: Limits how far a breach can spread
quiz.ex: Segmentation contains compromise to a zone.

quiz.p: A DMZ is used to…
o: Host internet-facing services separately from the internal network
quiz.ex: The DMZ isolates public-facing services.

quiz.p: Zero trust assumes…
o: No implicit trust — verify every access
quiz.ex: Zero trust verifies identity/authorisation regardless of location.

content.intro: Two services quietly make networks usable: DHCP hands out addressing, and DNS resolves names. Here they are from the network's point of view.

p: A client broadcasts for configuration and a DHCP server leases an IP, mask, gateway, and DNS. A DHCP relay forwards these broadcasts across subnets to a central server.
A resolver walks from root → TLD → authoritative servers (or uses a cache/forwarder) to turn a name into an IP. Caching makes repeat lookups fast.

note.text: Rogue DHCP servers and DNS spoofing are real risks — DHCP snooping and trusted resolvers (and DNSSEC where possible) mitigate them.

content.practice: Trace what a laptop receives from DHCP when it joins, and the steps to resolve a brand-new domain name.

quiz.p: A DHCP relay is needed when…
o: Every subnet has a DHCP server
Clients are on a different subnet from the DHCP server
quiz.ex: Relays forward DHCP across subnets to a central server.

quiz.p: DNS resolution generally proceeds…
quiz.ex: Resolvers go root → TLD → authoritative (with caching).

quiz.p: A rogue DHCP server is mitigated by…
quiz.ex: DHCP snooping permits DHCP only from trusted ports.

courses.title: Monitoring, Tools & Troubleshooting
courses.description: Find and fix network problems fast — essential CLI tools, a repeatable OSI-based method, packet analysis, and monitoring at scale.

content.intro: A handful of command-line tools diagnose the vast majority of network issues. Know what each proves.

ul.t: where along the path does it break?
local MAC mappings and active connections/ports.

note.text: ping the gateway, then a public IP, then a name: that quickly isolates local vs routing vs DNS problems.

content.practice: Run ping to your gateway and to 8.8.8.8, then nslookup a website — note which layer each result confirms.

quiz.p: Which tool shows the path and where it breaks?
quiz.ex: Traceroute reveals each hop and where it fails.

quiz.p: To test whether DNS is resolving you use…
quiz.ex: nslookup/dig query DNS directly.

quiz.p: Pinging 8.8.8.8 works but a website name fails — the likely problem is…
quiz.ex: IP works but names fail → DNS resolution issue.

content.intro: A structured method beats random changes — it finds root cause faster and avoids new problems.

p: Use the OSI model as a checklist — bottom-up (cable/link → IP → DNS → app) or top-down. Confirm each layer before moving on.

ul: Identify the problem and its scope (one user or many? what changed?)
Form a theory, then test it — one change at a time
Fix, verify, and document the cause

note.text: Change one variable at a time. Changing several at once hides which change actually fixed it.

content.practice: Take 'a user can't reach the shared drive' and write the layer-by-layer checks you'd run in order.

quiz.p: Using the OSI model to troubleshoot means…
quiz.ex: Work layer by layer to localise the fault.

quiz.p: When testing a theory you should change…
quiz.ex: One change at a time isolates cause and effect.

quiz.p: A key early question is…
o: Is it one user or many, and what changed?
quiz.ex: Scope and recent changes localise the problem.

content.intro: When higher-level tools aren't enough, a packet capture shows exactly what's on the wire.

p: Tools like Wireshark capture frames on an interface. Use capture/display filters (e.g. by IP, port, or protocol) to cut through the noise.

sections.caption: A TCP three-way handshake as seen in a capture: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK.

note.text: Confirm a handshake completes, spot retransmissions/resets, verify DNS/DHCP exchanges, or prove where a conversation stops.

content.practice: Describe what you'd expect to see in a capture if a TCP connection is being refused by the server.

quiz.p: A TCP connection starts with which exchange?
quiz.ex: The three-way handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

quiz.p: Display filters in a capture tool are used to…
quiz.ex: Filters narrow the capture to what matters.

quiz.p: Packet analysis is most useful when…
o: Higher-level tools can't explain the problem
quiz.ex: Captures reveal exactly what's happening on the wire.

content.intro: You can't fix what you can't see. Monitoring turns reactive firefighting into proactive operations.

ul.t: who's talking to whom and how much (traffic patterns).

p: Capture what 'normal' looks like, then alert on deviations — link saturation, error spikes, a device going quiet.

note.text: Good monitoring catches capacity and failure trends before users notice — and shortens outages when they happen.

content.practice: Pick one metric from SNMP, NetFlow, and syslog you'd alert on, and say what problem each would catch early.

quiz.p: Which protocol polls device health like interface and CPU stats?
quiz.ex: SNMP polls device health metrics.

quiz.p: NetFlow tells you…
o: Traffic patterns (who talks to whom, how much)
quiz.ex: Flow data reveals conversation and volume patterns.

quiz.p: The point of a baseline is to…
o: Know normal so you can alert on deviations
quiz.ex: Baselines make anomalies detectable.
